Continuing analytic Cauchy solutions through convex domains

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

Local analytic existence gives a solution near its initial surface. To reach a larger domain, we need to control the surfaces across which that solution continues, and to ensure that extensions constructed in different places agree. Convexity will serve both purposes: it keeps certain complex normal covectors away from the characteristic set and makes local extensions compatible.

We prove analytic Cauchy existence along a noncharacteristic complex hypersurface, continuation through a real boundary, a global theorem on convex domains, and a cone theorem whose existence neighborhood does not depend on the forcing.

Use ordinary complex derivatives . On an open , , let with holomorphic coefficients. Covectors are complex, and all norms in this lesson are Euclidean unless individual coordinate inequalities are written.

The full quantitative flat Cauchy proof is Analytic Cauchy data on small polydiscs, Theorems 4–5 and Corollary 6. Its germ uniqueness and its arbitrary-data polynomial will be used with their exact domains. Analytic pullback and cotangent directions, Lemma 3, proves the holomorphic inverse construction by uniformly convergent complex contraction iterates; its last step takes a real restriction. The same proof before that last step supplies the holomorphic inverse for a holomorphic map with invertible complex derivative. The supplied complex contour proofs, Sections 16.1–16.3, supply joint power series, the identity principle and holomorphic limits.

Making local solutions agree

A germ along a subset specifies an ordinary function germ at each of its points, with local representatives which give those same germs at neighboring points of the subset. Uniqueness of a germ along a hypersurface means equality after restricting to a sufficiently small common neighborhood of the entire hypersurface.

Lemma 1 (three gluing facts).

  1. Compatible holomorphic germs along a locally closed subset of an open Euclidean set have one holomorphic representative on an open neighborhood of that subset.
  2. Let be open and convex. Suppose a holomorphic function on extends to balls centered on , with agreement on each ball's intersection with . Those extensions agree on all their mutual intersections.
  3. Analytic continuation of a specified holomorphic germ along a fixed path is unique. If a continuous family of paths all starts in an open set carrying the specified initial function, and each path has a continuation represented on a neighborhood of its complete image, their endpoint germs form a locally holomorphic function of the endpoint whenever the paths vary continuously with that endpoint.

Proof of 1. Write the subset as . Local closedness makes open in its closure: each point has an ambient neighborhood in which is closed, and that neighborhood meets the closure only in . Thus is open and is closed in . All closures in this paragraph are relative to the original ambient open set.

Choose a compact exhaustion of with . For example, in ambient real coordinates take When is the whole space, omit the distance inequality. Empty initial sets cause no problem. The closed shell is compact. Cover it by finitely many open balls whose closures lie in a domain of a representative , and in . Use empty for nonpositive indices. This is possible because . All the ball closures form a locally finite family in : near a point in the interior of some , only finitely many shell indices can meet.

In , let be the set where the germs of and differ. The identity principle makes both agreement and disagreement unions of connected components of this open intersection. Consequently is closed relative to it. Therefore is closed in . It is disjoint from , by compatibility of the initial germs. The family of these sets is locally finite, so its union is closed: a neighborhood of any point meets only finitely many of them, and a finite union of closed sets is closed. On , the representatives agree on every overlap and define one holomorphic function. This open contains . The same construction for agreement neighborhoods proves uniqueness as a neighborhood germ when the point germs are unique.

Proof of 2. If balls and , with , intersect, then . A point of the segment from to lies strictly inside both balls: choose its distances from the endpoints smaller than . The coincident-center case is immediate. The segment belongs to , by convexity. Approximating this point by points of shows that the intersection of the balls meets . The ball intersection is convex and connected. Its two holomorphic functions agree on a nonempty open subset in , and hence everywhere by the identity principle. In particular, extensions at every point of a compact boundary glue to a neighborhood of the closure, using a finite ball cover and the original function.

Proof of 3. A continuation along a compact path can be described by finitely many holomorphic representatives on balls and a finite subdivision of the path, with each subarc in its ball and successive germs agreeing at their transition point. Such a subdivision follows from compactness: each path point has a parameter interval mapped into its germ domain, and a finite refinement has the required overlaps. Comparing two chains along the same path and refining both subdivisions propagates their initial germ equality through every transition by the identity principle on a smaller ball. This proves uniqueness.

For the last assertion, fix one endpoint and its path. Its complete compact image has a neighborhood on which one representative is available, by the stated hypothesis. All sufficiently nearby paths lie in that neighborhood: a finite subcover of the path image gives a positive distance margin, and uniform closeness follows from continuity on the compact parameter interval. Their starting points lie in a neighborhood where that representative agrees with the initial function. Uniqueness along each nearby path identifies its endpoint germ with this single representative. Thus the endpoint germs are locally represented by holomorphic functions, and their unique values glue on overlaps.

Analytic initial hypersurfaces

An analytic hypersurface is locally given by , where is holomorphic and . It is noncharacteristic for if This does not depend on its local defining function. Indeed another defining function is a nonvanishing holomorphic multiple of , by its first-order transverse Taylor expansion, and is homogeneous of degree .

Theorem 2 (Cauchy germs along a hypersurface). Let be an analytic noncharacteristic hypersurface, and let be holomorphic on . There is a unique holomorphic solution germ along satisfying This germ has a representative on an actual open neighborhood of all of .

Proof. Near a point of , reorder coordinates so that . The map has an invertible complex derivative. The supplied complex inverse proof gives holomorphic coordinates , with .

The full chain rule gives . Repeating this rule times, the terms in which no derivative hits a coefficient give the principal symbol Every term differentiating a coefficient has fewer than derivatives on the unknown. In particular, the coefficient of is , which is nonzero near the point after shrinking.

For a holomorphic function , its first normal Taylor coefficients at vanish exactly when with holomorphic. This follows by factoring the convergent Taylor series in , whose coefficients are holomorphic in by the circle formula. Such divisibility makes all derivatives of total order less than vanish on that plane. Conversely, those derivatives include its normal derivatives. The full chain rule makes vanishing of all these jets invariant under holomorphic coordinates.

Apply the flat analytic Cauchy theorem to , with forcing , after division by the nonzero leading coefficient. It gives a unique local germ with the zero normal jets. Local germs agree at every point of their common portion of , by the same flat uniqueness. An embedded analytic hypersurface is locally closed by its local defining equation, so Lemma 1(1) supplies the asserted neighborhood representative and uniqueness along .

A global solution from its canonical vertical paths

Theorem 5 (global analytic Cauchy existence on a convex domain). Let be open and convex, and suppose Assume (G11) throughout . For every holomorphic on , there is a unique holomorphic on with

Proof. Theorem 2, or the flat Cauchy theorem and Lemma 1(1), gives a solution on a neighborhood of the whole initial tangential ball. Its germs are unique.

Fix with , and write , . By (G20), . Choose sufficiently close to that The second condition follows from openness at . Translate the tangential coordinates by and rotate the normal coordinate by . Intersect the transformed with . This is convex and contains its initial tangential ball. It also contains the vertical segment , by convexity and (G22). Translation and a unit complex normal rotation preserve the covector norm condition (G11), as follows directly from (G6).

Lemma 4 therefore continues the initial solution along to . It supplies one holomorphic function on a neighborhood of this entire path. At , the initial solution already supplies such a neighborhood.

It remains to prove that these endpoint germs fit together. The path lies in by convexity, and depends continuously, uniformly for , on . For one fixed , its constructed solution neighborhood therefore contains every sufficiently nearby canonical path. At their starting points it agrees with the initial solution, after shrinking the endpoint neighborhood if needed. The uniqueness and stability statement of Lemma 1(3) identifies their endpoint germs with this one holomorphic function. The endpoint germs hence give a single holomorphic on . The equation holds locally everywhere, and the initial jets remain those of the initial solution.

Any two such solutions agree near the initial ball by the flat germ uniqueness, and hence on the connected set by the identity principle. This proves uniqueness.

Nonzero normal data holomorphic on the tangential ball are also allowed. Their polynomial is holomorphic on the rightmost domain in (G20). Apply Theorem 5 to , and then add . No boundedness of or the data on all of is required.

Solving in a cone and continuing across its vertex

A cone below is invariant under multiplication by positive real numbers; it need not be invariant under multiplication by complex numbers.

Corollary 6 (complex-cone solvability and continuation). Let be an open convex cone with Suppose has holomorphic coefficients in a neighborhood of zero, and There is a neighborhood of zero, independent of , such that every holomorphic on admits a holomorphic solution of on . If a holomorphic solution in a cone neighborhood of zero has forcing which extends holomorphically to a full neighborhood of zero, that solution also extends holomorphically to a full neighborhood of zero.

Proof of existence. Normalize in (G25), using homogeneity and division by the nonzero complex number . The resulting closed ball is compact and the polynomial is nonzero on it. Undoing the shift gives a solution on . Since , zero is an interior point of : its defining left side at zero is . Thus some neighborhood of zero lies in . All these choices depend only on the coefficient and domain hypotheses, not on .

Proof of continuation. Suppose is given on intersected with a neighborhood of zero, and with holomorphic across zero. Choose still smaller so that lies in the common full coefficient and forcing neighborhood and in the neighborhood used to define the domain of . On the slice , , the normal jets of are defined and holomorphic, by (G24). They define a polynomial in the shifted normal variable, holomorphic on all of .

The nonzero-data version of Theorem 5 now solves (G28) on the entire , with these jets. Its shifted solution agrees with near the initial slice by Cauchy uniqueness. The intersection is convex, connected and contains that slice, so the identity principle gives equality throughout the intersection. The shifted solution is holomorphic on , which contains a full neighborhood of zero.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 (basic) — all jets or normal jets. In coordinates with , prove directly that for is equivalent to with holomorphic. Explain why this implies every derivative of total order less than vanishes on .

Solution. Expand on a small product of disks. The circle coefficient formula makes each holomorphic. The normal derivative equals at , so precisely the first coefficients vanish. Factoring leaves a convergent holomorphic series for . Differentiating fewer than times leaves a positive power of in every Leibniz term, even when some derivatives are tangential. The conclusion is local at every point of and therefore holds along all of it.

Exercise 7 (advanced) — uniqueness along a path is not arbitrary-path independence. Give a holomorphic germ which can continue along loops to a different germ, and explain which additional argument in Theorem 5 prevents such ambiguity.

Solution. Start with the logarithm germ at , normalized to zero. Along the unit circle, its derivative is . The change in its value after one positive turn is . Local logarithm germs exist by integrating on disks avoiding zero, using the supplied primitive theorem, and their adjusted constants give the continuation along the circle. Thus fixed-path uniqueness alone does not identify endpoints of different paths. Theorem 5 specifies one path for each endpoint. Each path has a complete solution neighborhood; nearby paths stay there and begin in the same initial solution. The resulting local endpoint identification, proved in Lemma 1(3), is what yields one holomorphic function on the convex domain.

Exercise 8 (intermediate) — the zero-dimensional tangential case. Describe the assertions of Theorem 5 and Corollary 6 when .

Solution. There is no ; its norm is zero and the initial tangential ball is the point . Condition (G11) says that the leading coefficient of the scalar ordinary differential operator never vanishes on , since . Theorem 5 gives the unique holomorphic solution on the convex domain with its first derivatives prescribed at zero. The dome construction still uses ; its complex normal has real part one. In Corollary 6, the cone contains the positive imaginary ray, and the condition at zero is . A solution in that cone continues through its vertex whenever the forcing does. The preceding proofs apply with empty tangential coordinates and unchanged normal estimates.

Programme proofs and mathematical source

  • Analytic Cauchy data on small polydiscs, Theorems 4–5 and Corollary 6, supplies full quantitative flat existence, arbitrary-germ uniqueness and the polynomial for nonzero jets. Analytic pullback and cotangent directions, Lemma 3, supplies the actual complex contraction inverse and its holomorphic limit. Complex contour foundations, Sections 16.1–16.3, supplies the primitives, joint Taylor series and identity arguments, with its scalar calculus and integration prerequisites.
  • Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis, reprint of the second edition, Springer, 2003, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2, Theorems 9.4.6–9.4.8 and Corollary 9.4.9. The neighborhood gluing, fixed bottom neighborhood, continuation at the limiting parameter, endpoint compatibility and exercises are developed here in original exposition.
